procedural_history.originating_court: First Appellant (likely a government official) passed an order dated November 20, 1961, under Section 15 of the Bombay Land Requisition Act.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated November 20, 1961, passed by the first appellant under Section 15 of the Bombay Land Requisition Act, requisitioning land for a new village site for flood victims.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Respondents (landowners) filed a Special Civil Application No. 373 of 1961 in the Bombay High Court, Nagpur Bench, challenging the validity of the requisition order. The High Court allowed the petition and quashed the order, holding that the Act did not authorize requisitioning for a permanent purpose like establishing a new village site.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellants (Collector, Akola) appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the High Court's judgment and order dated August 28, 1962. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and remanded the matter to the High Court to decide the other questions raised in the petition that it had not previously addressed.

directions: set aside the order passed by the High Court
remand the matter to the High Court to decide those questions in accordance with law
make no order as to costs

issue.issue_text: Whether the power to requisition land under the Bombay Land Requisition Act, a temporary statute, can be exercised for a public purpose that is not temporary in nature, such as the permanent rehabilitation of flood sufferers.

facts: The government requisitioned land under the Bombay Land Requisition Act, a temporary statute, for the public purpose of establishing a new village to resettle flood victims.
The landowners challenged this, arguing that a temporary law could not be used for a permanent purpose like building a new village.
The High Court agreed with the landowners, reasoning that since the Act itself was temporary, any requisition under it must also be for a temporary purpose, and it quashed the order.
law: The key provision is Section 5(1) of the Bombay Land Requisition Act, which empowers the government to requisition 'any land for any public purpose'.
The Act itself is a temporary statute, meaning its legal force is limited to a specific period unless extended.
application: The Supreme Court analyzed the plain text of Section 5(1) and found that the phrase 'for any public purpose' is broad and does not contain any restriction, either express or implied, limiting its use to only temporary purposes.

The Court held that the High Court was wrong to 'confound the temporary life of the statute with the character of the purpose for which the power thereunder can be exercised'. In other words, the temporary nature of the law does not mean the purpose of the requisition must also be temporary.
The only limitation on the power is that the purpose must be a 'public purpose' and that the requisition itself ends when the Act expires.

The Court noted that the possibility of the land having to be returned to the owner upon the Act's expiration was a risk for the government and the new settlers to consider, but it did not invalidate the initial act of requisitioning the land for a non-temporary project.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the power to requisition under the Act could be exercised for any public purpose, regardless of whether that purpose was temporary or permanent. It held that the exercise of this power for the permanent rehabilitation of flood sufferers was valid and not an abuse of the Act, thereby overturning the High Court's decision.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the power to requisition land under the Bombay Land Requisition Act, a temporary statute, can be exercised for a public purpose that is not temporary in nature, such as the permanent rehabilitation of flood sufferers.
appellant_arguments: The High Court's interpretation of section 5(1) of the Act was incorrect and failed to appreciate the scope of its provisions.
The Act authorizes an order of requisitioning even if the public purpose for which it is made is not temporary.
The only requirement of section 5(1) is that the requisition be for a 'public purpose', and it does not specify that the purpose must be temporary.
respondent_arguments: Since the Act is a temporary statute, the power to requisition land under it can only be exercised for a temporary purpose, not a permanent one like establishing a new village.
An order for a permanent purpose could not have been in the contemplation of the temporary Act.
Exercising the power for a permanent purpose would render the operation of section 9 (regarding the return of land) impossible, which amounts to an abuse of power under the Act.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The temporary duration of a statute does not implicitly restrict the powers granted within it to only temporary purposes. When a statute authorizes an action for "any public purpose," the scope of that power is not limited to temporary purposes unless explicitly stated; the temporary life of the statute is distinct from the character of the purpose for which the power can be exercised.
obiter: If a requisitioning authority uses land for a purpose that is not temporary, it is the responsibility of the government and those who construct structures on the land to contemplate the future possibility of having to return the land to its owner.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that the High Court erred in holding that the power to requisition land under the temporary Bombay Land Requisition Act could only be exercised for a temporary public purpose. The court reasoned that the temporary nature of the statute only limits the duration for which the requisition can last, not the character of the public purpose itself. The phrase "for any public purpose" in section 5(1) is wide enough to include purposes that are not temporary in nature, and to interpret it otherwise is to wrongly conflate the temporary life of the Act with the nature of the purpose for which the power can be exercised.
legal_tests_applied: Plain reading of the statutory text, specifically section 5(1) of the Bombay Land Requisition Act.
why_appellant_won: The court determined that the words 'any land for any public purpose' in section 5(1) are sufficiently wide to include any public purpose, whether temporary or otherwise.

The court held that reading a limitation into the section that the purpose must be temporary is to 'confound the temporary life of the statute with the character of the purpose for which the power thereunder can be exercised.'

The court reasoned that section 9, which provides for the return of the land upon derequisition, does not limit the nature of the purpose under section 5(1). Section 9 simply dictates that the land must revert to the owner when the Act expires, regardless of the use to which it was put during the requisition period.
The court concluded that 'The hfe of the p<iwer and the purpose for Which · it is exerdised are two distinct ingredients of section 5(1) and ought not to be oonfu&OO.'
why_respondent_lost: The respondent's argument that a temporary statute can only be used for a temporary purpose was rejected as a misinterpretation of the law.

The respondent's contention that using the land for a permanent purpose would render the operation of section 9 (return of land) impossible, and thus constitute an abuse of power, was dismissed. The court clarified that the obligation to return the land upon the Act's expiry is absolute and is not affected by the nature of the use during the requisition period.
